title: Analysis: Global fossil-fuel emissions set to fall in 2026 amid Hormuz crisis - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief calculates global fossil-fuel CO2 will fall ~0.5% in 2026 because the Hormuz-driven oil and gas demand collapse — the IEA now sees oil demand down 2.5mbpd (-2.4%) versus a +930,000bpd forecast in January — more than offsets a 1.2% rise in coal demand, undercutting the 'return to coal' narrative. The piece argues the US-Iran war may be causing permanent oil demand destruction via record EV share gains and LNG-importing governments pivoting to domestic clean energy.

themes.theme: Hormuz crisis flips the 2026 emissions balance

insights.claim: Global fossil-fuel CO2 emissions are set to fall by around 0.5% in 2026, driven by the fallout from the Hormuz crisis rather than by climate policy.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: A geopolitically-driven emissions decline means the decarbonisation datapoint is a price shock, not structural policy — it can reverse if the strait reopens.

themes.theme: Permanent demand destruction and the peak-oil date

insights.claim: The IEA has moved from forecasting a 2027 oil demand rebound well above 2025 levels to expecting oil use to be effectively flat for two years.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Two flat years removes the rebound narrative underpinning upstream capex cycles and long-dated crude curves.
